sections.html:
Bozeman is the seat of Gallatin County, which fills a corner of southwest Montana. About 118,960 people lived here in 2020, behind only one other Montana county. Bozeman, Belgrade and Three Forks are cities, Manhattan and West Yellowstone are towns, and Big Sky, Gallatin Gateway and Four Corners are among the unincorporated communities. Big Sky Resort lies partly in Gallatin and partly in Madison County.

Jobs center on Montana State University and Bozeman Health. Since 2010 few Montana counties have added people faster, and Bozeman alone is forecast at 87,400 residents, close to half of the county's projected total. New arrivals and a young population turning over around the university keep houses in demand.

Values here are high enough that many primary residences cross the $378,000 line in the 2026 rate schedule, so they pay at more than one rate.

sections.h2: How Gallatin County homes are taxed in 2026
sections.html:
What you do with the house decides the rate. Live in it and the state charges 0.76 percent up to $378,000, then 0.90 percent through $756,000, then 1.10 percent through $1,511,999, then 1.90 percent for the rest. Use it as a vacation place, a short-term rental or a vacant lot and every dollar is charged 1.90 percent. After that, mills set by your city, school district and special districts convert the taxable value into a bill.

Homestead ruleWhat Montana requires
Homestead eligibilityOwner lives there at least 7 months of the year
Long-term rental eligibilityRented 28 or more days for at least 7 months a year
Rate after a saleStays through the calendar year; new owner must apply by March 1
Eligible homesSingle-family, townhome, condo, manufactured home with up to 1 acre

Because resort areas like Big Sky are inside county lines, double-check the class your property was in before pricing it. Someone moving in will probably want to claim the homestead rate for the following year.

sections.h2: When Gallatin County taxes are due
sections.html:
Gallatin County property tax arrives as one bill with two payment dates. Half comes due at 5 p.m. on November 30, or 30 days after the postmark if your notice went out late, and the remainder at 5 p.m. on May 31. The statute behind this is Montana Code 15-16-102.

Owner-occupants can sign up for seven nearly equal monthly payments, each due on a month's last day between November 30 and May 31. A missed installment turns delinquent right away, with the usual 2 percent penalty and monthly interest. Arrears from earlier years do not prevent you from paying this year's bill, but anything earmarked for delinquency gets applied to the oldest year first.

Selling mid-year? Find out from the title company which half is paid. The unpaid half and the share belonging to each party can shift the numbers on the closing statement.

Two offices split the work. Money questions belong to the county treasurer, who sits at 311 West Main, Room 103 in Bozeman and answers at 406-582-3033 or 406-582-3030. Value and class questions belong to the state's Bozeman Office, reachable at 406-582-3400 or dorgallatinoffice@mt.gov.

  • Treasurer: tax bills, payments, delinquent taxes, tax liens and assignments.
  • Department of Revenue Bozeman Office: appraisal, classification, corrections to property characteristics.
  • Clerk and Recorder: receives direct appeals to the county tax appeal board.
  • Title company: confirms what is owed and pays it at closing.

Check that the state has your current mailing address. Notices of pending liens are mailed to whatever address is on file, and an email to the Bozeman office will update it.

A payment made after the due date is late immediately and picks up a 2 percent penalty, plus interest of 5/6 of 1 percent each month. Montana Code 15-17-125 requires a lien on real property that is still unpaid by the first working day in August.

The sequence runs like this. A courtesy notice goes out once the first half is late. When the second half is late, a notice appears in the Bozeman Daily Chronicle, and about two weeks before that August date pending lien notices are mailed. If nothing has been paid by August 31, an outside party may take assignment of the lien by covering all taxes, penalty, interest and costs.

Bozeman adds a twist. The city forwards delinquent special assessments to the county for collection, so an owner can have paid county property tax and still face a lien for unpaid Bozeman special assessments.

  • August 1 (first working day): liens attach to still-delinquent properties.
  • August 15: earliest date an assignee may mail the required notice of pending assignment.
  • August 31: first day assignments can be purchased.
  • September 1: most assignments are issued.

sections.h2: Appealing a valuation and paying under protest
sections.html:
The deadline is 30 days after the date on the classification and appraisal notice. In that window you can send Form AB-26 to the Department of Revenue, or bypass it and go to the county tax appeal board through the clerk and recorder. A further appeal reaches the Montana Tax Appeal Board, and its rulings stand unless district court says otherwise.

Protecting a possible refund with interest takes two things: a written protest to the county treasurer, and full payment of the disputed tax before it turns delinquent. Evidence you bring this cycle is judged as of January 1, 2024.

sections.h2: Selling with a lien or unpaid assessments
sections.html:
You can still sell with a lien in place. The title company tracks down every open item, such as county tax, penalty, interest and Bozeman special assessments, and pays them out of your proceeds at closing. With a cash buyer no underwriter is waiting on a payoff letter.

Steps that help: request the treasurer's current balance early, ask whether the city has sent any special assessments to the county, and compare the final statement against both numbers before signing. If the house is rented or vacant, mention that to the buyer too, since it can affect which rate class applies from here on.

Many sellers ask whether the buyer inherits the old rate, and the answer is no, not for long. The rate class carries through the end of the calendar year, then the new owner has to apply. Passing along your last tax bill and any homestead approval gives them what they need to file. Buyers who will rent the house long term should apply too, and should plan on renting for at least seven months of the year.

faqs.q: Who sets my Gallatin County property value?
faqs.a: The Montana Department of Revenue. The county treasurer bills the tax, and the department's Bozeman Office at 406-582-3400 answers value and classification questions.

faqs.q: What happens on August 1 if my taxes are unpaid?
faqs.a: The county treasurer attaches a tax lien to real property with delinquent taxes as of the first working day in August, and files it with the Clerk and Recorder. A copy goes to the owner's recorded address.

faqs.q: Can I owe Bozeman special assessments even if I paid county tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Bozeman forwards delinquent special assessments to the county, and they become part of the county's collection process, so a lien can attach for them.

faqs.q: How much is the 2026 rate on a Gallatin County second home?
faqs.a: A flat 1.90 percent of market value applies to second homes, short-term rentals and vacant residential lots. A primary residence starts at 0.76 percent.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Gallatin County house for cash with a lien on it?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company pays the lien, penalty and interest from the sale proceeds at closing, and a cash buyer does not need lender approval to proceed.
